"A burly wag of the place, full of trick and grimace, came and poked his jests into the ribs of a scented, cream-colored valet, and a scuffle broke out" — Sambo and Adolph are authorized removals. The draft anonymizes both. Parseable on its own.

"the scented valet was knocked off, at a good sum, to the young gentleman who had fancied him" — "the young gentleman who had fancied him": the draft has the young exquisite say "I was wanting a valet... I heard St. Clare's lot was going" and his companion warns him off, but the draft never has the first exquisite say "I buy him, that's flat!" as the source does. "He paused before the scented valet; spat a discharge of tobacco-juice upon the well-blacked boots; umph!—and walked on." — The source has "He paused a moment before Dolph; then spitting a discharge of tobacco-juice on his well-blacked boots, and giving a contemptuous umph, he walked on." The fellow-servant disappears — but Adolph is an authorized removal, so any residual seam from dropping Adolph is expected.

Let me check the "Mr. Skeggs" name at the end of the men's-room scene. After introducing him with role ("Mr. Skeggs, the keeper of a depot"), he is later referred to again: "the worthy Mr. Skeggs is busy and bright." This is fine — he was introduced with his role.

Everything appears structurally sound in both drafts.
